title: Branch and price for the length-constrained cycle partition problem
contribution: Branch and price for the length-constrained cycle partition problem with a set-partitioning model, bidirectional labeling that extends in one direction only and is proved correct under dominance, symmetry breaking, early branching and parallel pricing; 14.6 times faster than the previous branch and cut and 13 open instances closed (up to 76 nodes).
problem_entry: Compact MTZ and SEC models solved LCCP only up to 29 and 52 nodes and suffer from symmetry, weak relaxations and ineffective branching; the paper enters with a set-partitioning model over length-feasible cycles (pp. 1–2).
key_idea: Column generation with a labeling pricer per start node; symmetric travel times allow bidirectional search with extensions in one direction only (labels extended while t < q/2, then merged), plus index-based symmetry breaking, heuristic pricing, early branching by objective integrality and set covering under the triangle inequality (pp. 2–8).
assumptions: Undirected graph, critical times q_i > 0, travel times t_ij ≥ 0, possibly non-metric; binary set partitioning over exponentially many cycles; Lemma 3 assumes the triangle inequality; the 84 benchmark instances of [11] with 14–100 nodes plus a metric-closed copy (pp. 2–4, 8, 10).
proof_devices: Feasibility pruning t(ℓ) > q(ℓ) by induction over extensions (p. 4)
Dominance Lemma 1 (same end node, reduced cost and time no larger, node set a subset) with proof (p. 5)
Lemma 2: correctness of bidirectional search with dominance via the first forward label past the halfway point and substitution of a dominating label in the merge (p. 6)
Lagrangian bound rounded up by objective integrality; early branching when the child's first RMP value rounds up to the parent's bound (p. 7)
Lemma 3 (zero-dual nodes can be ignored under the triangle inequality) stated without proof; strong NP-hardness of the pricing problem claimed without proof (pp. 3, 8)
experiments: 84 instances, 2 h, Xeon Gold 5122; arms bnc-sec (predecessor on Gurobi 10.0.3), bnp-basic, bnp-full and four one-technique-off ablations, all started from the MCV solution; shifted geometric mean of time (shift 1 s) on instances solved by at least one arm: bnc-sec 142.8 s and 39 solved, bnp-full 9.8 s and 52, ablations 1.3–4.4 times slower; root column generation converged on 56 of 84; root gap 1.1% against 23.6%; metric-closed set slower for both arms, 55 solved and 7.5 s when the triangle inequality is exploited; one run per instance, no seeds; Gurobi thread count not stated (pp. 8–10).
positioning: Supersedes Hoppmann-Baum et al. [9, 11], criticised for symmetry; borrows from vehicle-routing branch-price-and-cut, bidirectional labeling, kidney-exchange cycle models and Mehrotra–Trick early branching (pp. 2, 5, 7).
writing: Contributions listed by section with the 14.6 headline up front; three numbered questions plus one asked out of curiosity; a counter-intuitive result flagged as such; the conclusion concedes that the gain depends on nontrivial techniques (pp. 3, 8, 10).
limits_future: Root column generation fails on 28 of 84 instances; start-heuristic bounds rarely improved when both arms time out; future: cutting planes inside branch and price and transfer to kidney exchange; numerical safety not named (pp. 9–10).

title: The SCIP optimization suite 10.0
contribution: Release report of the SCIP Optimization Suite 10.0, which ships a numerically exact solving mode for rational MILPs with VIPR certificates (main author Eifler, with contributions and revisions by Gleixner and Kamp) besides implied-integer detection, reflection symmetries, cut-based conflict analysis, GCG 4.0, PaPILO 3.0 and MIP-DD 2.0; exact mode 2.6–3.6 times slower than feature-matched and 6.8–10.8 times slower than default floating-point SCIP.
problem_entry: Floating-point solvers by design cannot guarantee results unaffected by roundoff nor produce independently verifiable certificates; the report highlights the features of the new release (pp. 2, 6–7).
key_idea: Exact mode as hybrid precision: safe directed-rounding floating point replaces symbolic computation at many places, exact LP only as fallback and at scheduled points, exact repair of heuristic solutions, VIPR certificates; per-plugin safety flags so that only plugins marked safe run in exact mode (pp. 7–11).
assumptions: Exact mode restricted to MILPs with rational data read exactly from MPS, LP, CIP, OPB/WBO and ZIMPL files; release test sets: 349 MILPs that previous releases could solve × 3 seeds and 169 MINLPLib instances × 5 seeds; exact evaluation on the MIPLIB 2017 benchmark set with 3 seeds; Hoffman–Kruskal argument for implied integrality (pp. 3–4, 7–8, 11–13).
proof_devices: Implied integrality via a network or transposed-network (totally unimodular) submatrix and Hoffman–Kruskal integrality of the y-subproblem for every integer fixing of x (pp. 12–13)
Floating-point bounds kept as safe outward roundings of the exact bounds (p. 8)
Safe dual bounds by bound shift and project-and-shift with exact-LP fallback and scheduled exact LPs (root end, depths 2^k, near-integral solutions, bounds near the cutoff, all integers fixed) (p. 9)

VIPR derivations by conic combination, Chvátal–Gomory rounding and disjunction with unsplitting; presolve uncertified, primal bound checked in the original space; C++ checker and a CakeML/HOL4 verified checker (pp. 10–11)
Exact repair of floating-point heuristic solutions: fix the rounded integers, solve the remaining LP exactly (p. 10)
PaPILO column dominations compressed into a directed forest so that transactions never conflict (p. 34)
experiments: SCIP 10.0 against 9.0 and against bugfix 9.2.4, Xeon Gold 5122, one single-threaded run per machine, 5400 s MILP and 3600 s MINLP, shifts 1 s and 100 nodes, subsets all, affected, brackets and both-solved, with runs with numerically inconsistent results removed from 'all' (1 of 1047 MILP, 36 and 29 of 845 MINLP by the tables); MILP time 0.98 and 0.96, MINLP 0.94 and 0.91 (MINLP with CPLEX 12.10 as LP solver); exact-mode table taken from Eifler's dissertation: 161/235/342 solved (exact/fp-reduced/fp-default), slowdown 2.6 and 3.6 against fp-reduced and 10.8 and 6.8 against fp-default (one-solved/both-solved); implied integers detected for 18.8% of variables but performance-neutral, so off by default; the CONOPT text swaps the time and node changes of Table 8 (pp. 4–7, 11–14, 19, 25).
positioning: Exact mode set against virtually all floating-point MIP solvers and built on the Cook–Koch–Steffy–Wolter and Jarck prototype; the implied-integer result contrasted with Gurobi's published gain; conflict analysis and delta debugging imported from pseudo-Boolean, SAT and SMT practice (pp. 6, 9, 13, 17, 38–39).
writing: Feature-by-feature report with exact parameter names, a reason for every feature shipped off by default, and a contributions-of-the-authors section; the exact-mode summary 'between 3 and 4' and 'around 10' rounds the measured 2.6/3.6 and 10.8/6.8 (pp. 7–11, 13, 19–21, 32, 39–40).
limits_future: Exact mode: MILP only, presolve certified only for binary programs with integer data, strong branching unsafe, only GMI cuts, about 10 times slower than default; implied integrality not yet exploited; several features off by default; future: exploit implied integrality, deterministic parallel pricing, an exact mode for the verified pseudo-Boolean categories (pp. 7, 9, 11, 13, 19–21, 32, 39).

title: Hybrid genetic search for dynamic vehicle routing with time windows
contribution: Adapts Hybrid Genetic Search to the dynamic VRPTW of the EURO meets NeurIPS 2022 competition (variable-size giant tours, a normalized fitness with a lateness term, dispatch-changing local search) without pre-training; median cost 7.82% below the best organizer baselines on the 250 competition instances.
problem_entry: Any VRPTW method can be lifted to the dynamic setting by fixing the dispatched subset per epoch; the paper instead decides dispatch and routes in an integrated way inside HGS, without training (p. 2).
key_idea: Make HGS work on variable-size solutions: variable giant tours, an initial population with random removal of optional customers, ordered crossover on variable sizes, a fitness normalized by dispatched nodes and epoch progress plus a lateness term, and delete, add and swap-out operators (pp. 4–5).
assumptions: VRPTW with time windows, demands and capacity; DVRPTW over epochs with must-go customers; the 250 competition instances; no assumption stated for the fitness design (pp. 1–2, 5).
proof_devices: n/a for proofs; design devices follow
Fitness (p_dist S_dist + p_cap S_cap + p_time S_time + p_late S_late) / (((t − 1)/T + 1)(n + 1)) with p_late = 100 (pp. 4–5)
Initial population from random orderings with optional customers removed with probabilities {0, 0.1, 0.5, 1} (p. 4)
Delete, add and swap-out operators run before the original route-improvement heuristics (p. 5)
experiments: 250 competition instances; organizer baselines (greedy, lazy, random, oracle, supervised, dqn) that all use HGS and differ only in the dispatch strategy; Xeon Gold 5122, single-threaded, 5 min per epoch; violin plot; median cost 7.82% below greedy and dqn and 10.37% above the oracle; better than the oracle on 7 instances, worse than greedy and dqn on 19, worst of all on 3 (stuck at the trivial start solution); no seeds, no test behind 'significantly', no ablation (pp. 5–6).
positioning: Exact branch-price-and-cut reaches about 200 customers, hence metaheuristics; HGS won the 12th DIMACS challenge; learned baselines lose to greedy while the top competition entries were ML-based (pp. 1–2, 6).
writing: Short proceedings paper; motivation set by contrast; failures given with counts and a cause; unedited sentences remain in the preprint (pp. 2, 4, 6).
limits_future: Higher variance than the baselines, with counted bad cases and their cause; future: combine ML-based customer selection with DHGS (p. 6).

title: Combining precision boosting with LP iterative refinement for exact linear optimization
contribution: Precision boosting embedded as a fallback inside LP iterative refinement in SoPlex: refinement runs in double precision and boosts only on numerical trouble, stalling or contradicted status claims; it solves as many LPs as pure boosting, is faster than it, and removes all failed exact-LP calls in exact SCIP with a small speed-up.
problem_entry: Iterative refinement beats precision boosting in most cases but has no reliable recovery when the floating-point LP fails, as seen on pure LPs and in exact MIP branch and cut (pp. 1–2).
key_idea: Keep refinement as the main loop, boost precision only on three failure types and restart refinement at the higher precision with re-approximated data, scaled zero tolerances and stored warm-start bases; feasibility and optimality tolerances stay fixed (pp. 5–8).
assumptions: LP min{cᵀx | Ax = b, x ≥ ℓ} with rational A of full row rank, zero tolerances, simplex methods; limited-precision LP oracle (4a)–(4d) for convergence; test sets lplib, cutlib (100 hard LPs from exact SCIP) and 132 MIPLIB 2017 benchmark instances × 3 seeds (pp. 2, 8–9).
proof_devices: Failure triggers: non-optimal status or residuals near one, stalling (two iterations with violation reduction below a factor 2^4), infeasibility or unboundedness claims contradicted by exactly solved auxiliary LPs (pp. 5–6)
Zero tolerances 10^(−⌊p′c⌋) with p′ = p log 2/log 10, c = 1 and c = 0.625 (p. 7)
Warm-start bases stored at power-of-two iteration counts and at least every 10,000 iterations (p. 7)

Convergence argument: arbitrary precision makes a limited-precision oracle constructible, so refinement converges with a fixed η < 1; detailed proof beyond scope, conditioned on a backward-stable LU update (Bartels–Golub, not Forrest–Tomlin) (pp. 8–9)
experiments: SoPlex 6.0.3, GMP 6.1.2, Xeon Gold 5122, 7200 s; settings ir-double, boosting-pure and ir-boosting, all with a final-basis factorization; only LPs whose initial basis is not optimal (84 lplib, 91 cutlib), timed after the shared initial solve; solved 79/44/79 and 91/26/91; the all-solved subset is biased toward ir-double, as stated; a text slip (17.3% 'faster than ir-double' where Table 2 gives 31.1% faster than boosting-pure); MIP: 146 boosted instance-seed runs, boosting 3.8% and 4.4% faster, exact-LP failures 5.4 and 50.8 reduced to 0.0 (pp. 9–13).
positioning: A natural combination of QSopt_ex-style precision boosting (Applegate, Cook, Dash, Espinoza) with the authors' own iterative refinement; first implementation of both in one LP solver; the literature lacks a convergence proof for pure boosting (pp. 2, 8–9).
writing: Literature expectation stated before the test; a hope stated before the MIP test (boosting may remove the need for cut weakening) answered against itself (a complementary technique); a theoretical claim on an intuitive argument; two definitions of speed-up in one section (pp. 8–9, 12–13).
limits_future: No quad-precision step; boosting from the start is often faster on cutlib; the rational LU of the final basis can be a major bottleneck; future: roundoff-error-free LU factorization and a 128-bit step (pp. 6, 10–11, 14).

title: Scylla: a matrix-free fix-propagate-and-project heuristic for mixed-integer optimization
contribution: Scylla, a feasibility-pump-like MIP heuristic that replaces LP solves by a few warm-started PDLP iterations under a loose, geometrically tightened tolerance and rounds by fix-and-propagate; it loses to a simplex-based feasibility pump overall but finds solutions in 42 more instance-seed runs and is about four times faster when the root LP takes more than 60 s.
problem_entry: LP-based heuristics assume optimal LP solutions and cheap re-optimization, which fails during presolving (no LP solution yet), in applications with costly simplex re-optimization, and for large stand-alone use (pp. 1–2).
key_idea: A feasibility pump with the projection replaced by limited-precision PDHG (PDLP) and rounding by fix-and-propagate, plus an objective update toward an ℓ1 distance; matrix-free, using only sparse matrix-vector products (pp. 2–4).
assumptions: General MIP min{cᵀx : Ax ≥ b, ℓ ≤ x ≤ u, x_j ∈ Z for j ∈ I}; 283 instances from MIPLIB 2017 and the FP 2.0 set after removing those solved in SCIP presolve (the MIPLIB 2017 subset is not stated) (pp. 3, 5).
proof_devices: n/a for proofs; design devices follow
PDLP stopping tolerance ε^(1) = 0.01 and ε^(K+1) = max{0.98 ε^(K), 10^-8}, warm start from the previous primal-dual pair (pp. 3–4)
Objective update ĉᵀx = α^K (√|I|/‖c‖) cᵀx + (1 − α^K) Δ(x, x̂^(K)) with α = 0.9 (Algorithm 1.1, p. 3; p. 4)
Fix-and-propagate that continues past empty domains and always returns an integer point; random perturbation on cycling (p. 4)
experiments: Baseline: the open-source feasibility pump of [16] with SoPlex 6.0.2, extended with PDLP; Xeon Gold 6338, 3600 s, ten seeds, 2830 instance-seed runs; metrics: solutions found, wins, shifted geometric means of gap and time (shifts not stated), model-building overhead; overall the FP is better (gap 27.46 against 40.92, time 10.06 s against 17.30 s); root LP 1–60 s: the FP finds more solutions, Scylla is faster; root LP above 60 s: Scylla 205 against 163 solutions found and 234.80 s against 974.66 s ('nearly four times', table ratio 4.15) (pp. 5–6).
positioning: Continues the feasibility-pump line (Fischetti, Glover and Lodi; Bertacco et al.; Achterberg and Berthold; FP 2.0) and fix-and-propagate heuristics; builds on PDLP (pp. 2–4).
writing: The overall loss reported first and explained; implementation overhead separated from the method; the claim restricted to the subset with hard root LPs (pp. 5–6).
limits_future: Loses on the whole test set; the OR-Tools interface rebuilds the model in every iteration; the parallelism of sparse matrix-vector products is unused; future: multithreaded sparse BLAS, MIQPs with diagonal Hessian, an ℓ2 distance (pp. 5–6).
